rows.verified: HSE defines manual handling as transporting or supporting a load by hand or bodily force, including lifting, lowering, pushing, pulling, carrying or moving it.
Employers must avoid hazardous manual handling so far as reasonably practicable.
Hazardous manual-handling operations that cannot be avoided must be assessed for injury risk.
Risks from unavoidable manual handling must be reduced as low as reasonably practicable.
Manual-handling law does not set a universal specific weight limit.
Where injury risk exists and it is reasonably practicable, information may be required about a load's weight and centre-of-gravity position.
Hazardous handling can be avoided by redesigning tasks or automating or mechanising material movement.
Risk reduction can include mechanical aids and changes to the task, load, workplace layout, carrying distance, work rate, lighting and floor conditions.
Manual-handling risk depends on the load, posture, frequency, distance, worker capability, environment and available controls.
HSE manual-handling guidance is task-, load-, worker-, workplace-, control- and time-specific and is not an exact parcel-level injury probability.
The Control of Noise at Work Regulations 2005 require employers to prevent or reduce health and safety risks from workplace noise.
Employers must assess employees' risks from noise exposure.
Employers must take action to reduce noise exposure that creates risk.
Hearing protection must be provided when exposure cannot be reduced enough by other methods.
Employers must ensure statutory noise exposure limits are not exceeded.
Workers must receive relevant information, instruction and training about workplace-noise risks and controls.
Health surveillance is required where noise exposure creates a risk to health.
Daily or weekly exposure action values are 80 dB(A) and 85 dB(A), while the exposure limit value is 87 dB(A), after permitted hearing-protection effects.
Noise risk depends on sound level, peak pressure, duration, frequency content, task, hearing protection, worker susceptibility and exposure history.
HSE noise evidence is workplace-, task-, worker-, control-, measurement- and time-specific and is not an exact parcel-level hearing-loss probability.
Workplace-transport accidents can involve people being struck, run over or crushed by vehicles, plant or trailers, and falls from vehicles.
Risk assessments must include workplace-transport activities such as loading and unloading.
Mapping vehicle and pedestrian movements can identify locations where they interact.
Site improvements should reduce contact between pedestrians and vehicles, including separate routes where possible.
One-way systems and layouts that avoid reversing should be considered where practicable.
